common_name: Möwe Hydrangea (Teller Series Deep Rose-Red Lacecap, syn. 'Seagull')

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in rich, moist, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade; Möwe (German for 'seagull', often anglicized 'Mowe') is one of the earliest Teller-series lacecaps bred at the Swiss federal horticultural research station in Wädenswil, released in 1964, well before later series siblings like 'Nachtigall'.

directions: Möwe is one of the original Teller-series lacecaps from the Wädenswil breeding program, flowering with flat heads of deep rose-red sterile florets ringing a cream-colored fertile center, the color intensifying toward true red in alkaline soil and shifting paler pink to blue where soil is more acidic. It forms a sturdy, upright shrub reaching about five feet and has gone on to figure as a breeding parent behind several later Teller introductions. Grow in rich, humus-laden, consistently moist soil with some afternoon shade, since full baking sun can scorch the flower heads in hot climates. Prune only right after flowering, since next year's buds set on the current season's old wood over summer.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society) — Hydrangea Section Macrophyllae Cultivars M
Heritage Hydrangeas Nursery — Hydrangea macrophylla Möwe

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in rich, moist, well-drained soil with afternoon shade; Bodensee was bred in Germany around 1950 by Brugger, predating and separate from the Swiss Teller-series breeding program, though it has occasionally been crossed into later German and Swiss hydrangea breeding lines.

directions: Bodensee produces full, rounded mophead flower heads that run deep pink to red in alkaline soil and shift toward purer blue in acidic soil, held on a vigorous shrub that can reach about five feet tall and wide. Unusually for an older German mophead, it sometimes reblooms with a second flush later in the season rather than flowering only once in early summer. Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with afternoon shade, since the paler green foliage can scorch under hot, direct sun. Limit pruning to right after the main bloom flush to protect the following year's old-wood flower buds.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society) — Hydrangea Section Macrophyllae Cultivars B

common_name: Eisvogel Hydrangea (Kingfisher, Teller Series Deep Blue-to-Pink Lacecap)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in rich, moist, well-drained soil with afternoon shade; Eisvogel (German for 'kingfisher') is a 1979 Teller-series release from the Swiss federal breeding program in Wädenswil, introduced the same year as series relative 'Nachtigall'.

directions: Eisvogel is a free-flowering Teller-series lacecap whose large sterile ray florets shift between deep blue and strong pink depending heavily on soil pH, framing a fertile center that opens slightly earlier than many series relatives. It grows into a compact shrub around five feet tall and is valued by cutting gardeners since its flower heads hold up well when dried. Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil with afternoon shade to protect bloom color from fading in harsh sun. Prune lightly right after flowering, since buds for next year's bloom form on the current season's old wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society) — Hydrangea Section Macrophyllae Cultivars E–F

common_name: Alyne Fisher Daylily (Parent of Little Infant's Breeding Line, Cream Blend)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Alyne Fisher descends from a cross of 'Shells Of Dallas' and 'Little Infant', the 1977 Annie T. Giles Award winner, and divides congested clumps well every three to four years.

directions: Registered by Ury Winniford in 1982 and named for Alyne Fisher of Austin, Texas, this semi-evergreen daylily bears cream flowers about four inches across, brushed with pink and a soft rose halo above a green throat, carried on compact 16-inch scapes. It opens early in the season, well ahead of most midseason daylilies, giving gardens color before many other cultivars have started to bloom. Its small stature and modest spread make it a good fit for edging or small container plantings rather than the back of a border. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Region 6 — Histories of Daylily Names

common_name: Inez Tarrant Daylily (Parent of Little Infant's Breeding Line, Orchid Pink Self)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Inez Tarrant descends from a cross of 'Future Forecast' and 'Little Infant', the 1977 Annie T. Giles Award winner, and divides congested clumps well every three to four years.

directions: Registered by Ury Winniford in 1982 and named for Inez Tarrant of Jones Creek, Texas, herself a prolific daylily hybridizer who went on to register about 50 cultivars, this semi-evergreen daylily carries orchid-pink self flowers roughly five inches across with a green throat, on 20-inch scapes. It blooms in the early-midseason, filling a slightly later gap than its sibling-line cultivars bred from the same 'Little Infant' parentage. The clean, unmarked pink coloring and medium stature make it a versatile mixer in perennial borders. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Region 6 — Histories of Daylily Names

common_name: Spacecoast Sweet Eye Daylily (Offspring of Spacecoast Sweetness, Pink with Rose Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Spacecoast Sweet Eye was bred from a cross of 'Spacecoast Sweetness' x seedling, extending the Annie T. Giles Award-winning Spacecoast Sweetness breeding line into a patterned, eyed form.

directions: Registered by John L. Kinnebrew Jr. in 2002, Spacecoast Sweet Eye is a tetraploid daylily whose wide, overlapping, delicately ruffled petals open pink with a darker rose eye and picotee edge above a green throat, on scapes reaching two to three feet with four-way branching. It blooms in the early-midseason and reblooms reliably through summer, improving on the simple pink self of its parent 'Spacecoast Sweetness' with a more patterned, eyed look. The evergreen foliage suits warmer climates especially well, and the plant tolerates full sun to partial shade. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Hemerocallis 'Spacecoast Sweet Eye'

common_name: Copper Windmill Daylily (Parent of All American Windmill, Fragrant Copper-Orange Spider)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Copper Windmill was later crossed with 'Yellow Angel' to produce the 1995 cultivar 'All American Windmill', which went on to win the Lambert/Webster Award in 2004.

directions: Registered by Clarence J. Crochet in 1989, Copper Windmill is a diploid spider daylily with fragrant copper-orange flowers about seven inches across and a green throat, carried on 27-inch scapes. Each bloom stays open longer than 16 hours, an extended-bloom trait that lets gardeners enjoy the flowers well into the evening. It opens in midseason and earned an Honorable Mention from the American Hemerocallis Society in 2000. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Yellow Angel Daylily (Parent of All American Windmill, Fragrant Yellow Spider)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow Angel was later crossed with 'Copper Windmill' to produce the 1995 cultivar 'All American Windmill', which went on to win the Lambert/Webster Award in 2004. Not to be confused with the unrelated, later-registered 'Yellow Angel Wings' (2013).

directions: Registered by Lennington-Long in 1989, Yellow Angel is a fragrant spider daylily with vibrant yellow flowers roughly ten inches across and a green throat, held on 30-inch scapes. It blooms in the mid-to-late season, extending color later in the year than many of its earlier-flowering spider relatives. Its narrow, widely spaced petals give it the loose, airy look typical of large unusual-form spider daylilies. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Stellar Double Rose Daylily (Parent of Amanda's Little Red Shoes, Red Double with White Edge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Stellar Double Rose was later crossed with 'Reba My Love' to produce Nancy Eller's 2004 cultivar 'Amanda's Little Red Shoes', winner of the Ida Munson Award in 2013.

directions: Registered by Brown in 1995, Stellar Double Rose is a fragrant, dormant daylily with fully double red flowers about five inches across, deepened by a darker red eyezone and finished with a thin, lightly ruffled white edge, on 39-inch scapes. It blooms in the early-to-midseason with dependable rebloom and earned an Honorable Mention from the American Hemerocallis Society. Its dormant foliage habit and cold tolerance suit it especially well to prolonged-winter climates where many evergreen daylilies struggle. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Birds of a Feather Daylily (Parent of Pumpkin Britches, Fragrant Light Red)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Birds of a Feather was later crossed with 'Dances with Giraffes' to produce Eric Simpson's 2016 cultivar 'Pumpkin Britches', winner of the Lambert/Webster Award in 2022.

directions: Registered by Shooter-E. in 2007, Birds of a Feather is a fragrant, dormant diploid daylily bearing light red flowers about ten inches across above a large, dark green starburst pattern that fades to a yellow throat, on 37-inch scapes carrying about 22 buds across four branches. It blooms in the early-midseason with reliable rebloom, giving a long season of color from a single clump. Its unusually wide bloom size for a diploid daylily helped make it a useful parent for later large-flowered unusual-form breeding. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: Stout Gardens at Dancingtree nursery catalog
